```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(infer)
library(broom)

mario <- mariokart |>
  filter(total_pr < 100) |>
  mutate(price = total_pr,
         cond_new = if_else(cond == "new", 1, 0),
         stock_photo = if_else(stock_photo == "yes", 1, 0)) |>
  select(price, cond_new, stock_photo, duration, wheels)
```

## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 27: Applications: Model and infer](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to fit and read one-predictor and multiple regression models of eBay auction prices for *Mario Kart*, to test and estimate a slope by permutation and by the bootstrap, and to compare two models with cross-validation.

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `applications-model-and-infer`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it.

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

## Mathematical approach to linear models

All other characteristics held constant, are longer auctions associated with higher or lower prices? This section answers with the mathematical model: a regression on the game's condition alone, then one that adds three more predictors.

The tibble has 143 rows, one per auction, and 12 variables. The chapter, though, says the `mariokart` dataset includes results from 141 auctions.

###

The first four rows match the chapter's table, starting with a new game, shown with a stock photo, that sold for \$51.55 over 3 days with one wheel. `cond_new` and `stock_photo` are *indicator variables*, taking only the values 0 and 1, similar to `bankruptcy` in the `loans` dataset.

### Exercise 4

Start a new chunk with a linear regression of `price` on `cond_new`, using `mario`. Show the full table of coefficients. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-approach-to-linear-models-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-approach-to-linear-models-4-test
#| echo: true
lm(price ~ cond_new, data = mario) |>
  tidy()
```

###

The slope is 10.90 with a standard error of 1.26, and its p-value, about $10^{-14}$, means there is strong evidence that the coefficient is different from zero when using this one-variable model. The 10.90 model coefficient predicts a price of an extra \$10.90 for those games that are new versus those that are used.

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk with a table that shows the estimate and standard error of the `cond_new` coefficient from both models: the one with `cond_new` alone and the one with all four predictors. Render.


```{r}
#| label: mathematical-approach-to-linear-models-9-test
#| echo: true
bind_rows(
  "One predictor" = lm(price ~ cond_new, data = mario) |>
    tidy(),
  "Four predictors" = lm(price ~ cond_new + stock_photo + duration + wheels,
                         data = mario) |>
    tidy(),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  filter(term == "cond_new") |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error)
```

###

The new-game premium falls from \$10.90 to \$5.13 once wheels and the rest are in the model. The one-predictor model was biased by the confounding variable `wheels`.

### Exercise 10

Replace the table with a plot of every coefficient except the intercepts from both models, each with its 95% confidence interval, coloring the two models differently. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-approach-to-linear-models-10
```

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-approach-to-linear-models-10-test
#| echo: true
bind_rows(
  "One predictor" = lm(price ~ cond_new, data = mario) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE),
  "Four predictors" = lm(price ~ cond_new + stock_photo + duration + wheels,
                         data = mario) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = term, y = estimate, color = model)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.4))
```

###

Only `cond_new` appears in both models, and its two intervals, 8.41 to 13.4 and 3.05 to 7.21, do not even overlap. The intervals for `stock_photo` and `duration` cross zero, while the one for `wheels` sits well above it.

```{r}
bind_rows(

) |>

  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model),
         term = fct_recode(term,
                           "New condition" = "cond_new",
                           "Stock photo" = "stock_photo",
                           "Each day of auction" = "duration",
                           "Each Wii wheel" = "wheels")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = term, y = estimate, color = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "What Adds to the Price of Mario Kart on eBay",
       subtitle = "Holding wheels and the rest constant cuts the premium for a new game from $10.90 to $5.13",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Change in Total Price, with 95% Confidence Interval",
       color = "Model",
       caption = "141 eBay auctions under $100, October 2009; two bundles removed") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

###

When we use both variables, this particular underlying and unintentional bias is reduced or eliminated (though bias from other confounding variables may still remain). Each extra wheel adds \$7.29, more than a new game does once wheels are held constant.

## Computational approach and cross-validation

Previously, using a mathematical model, we investigated the coefficients associated with `cond_new` when predicting `price` in a linear model. This section tests and estimates that slope by permutation and by the bootstrap, then compares the one- and four-predictor models by cross-validation.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that uses **infer** to calculate the slope of `price` on `cond_new` in `mario`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-1-test
#| echo: true
mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")
```

###

The same 10.9 as the regression table, because **infer** fits the same least squares line. $\beta_1$ represents the population value for the difference in price between new *Mario Kart* games and used games.

### Exercise 2

Replace the code in that chunk so that it uses **infer** to create 1,000 permuted datasets, in which `price` is shuffled across `cond_new` under the null hypothesis of no relationship, and calculates the slope for each. Set a seed first. Store the result as `null_slopes` and print it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-2-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(47)
null_slopes <- mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

null_slopes
```

###

We use the chapter's seed, 47, and a different seed gives slightly different slopes. When the data are randomly permuted, prices are randomly assigned to a condition (new or used), so that the null hypothesis is forced to be true.

### Exercise 3

Replace the print with a summary of `null_slopes`: the smallest slope, the largest slope, and the number of slopes at least as far from zero as the observed 10.9. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-3-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(47)
null_slopes <- mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

null_slopes |>
  summarize(min = min(stat),
            max = max(stat),
            as_extreme = sum(abs(stat) >= 10.9))
```

###

Our permuted slopes run from -6.79 to 5.59, and not one of the 1,000 reaches 10.9. Because the observed slope is not a plausible value under the null distribution, the p-value is essentially zero.

### Exercise 4

Replace the summary with a histogram of `null_slopes`, with a vertical red line at the observed slope of 10.9. Render.

```{r}

  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

null_slopes |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10.9, color = "red")
```

###

The red line sits far to the right of every permuted slope, as in the chapter's figure. The regression table's p-value was also essentially zero, and often, the mathematical and computational approaches to inference will give quite similar answers.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk so that it uses **infer** to draw 1,000 bootstrap samples from `mario` and calculates the slope of `price` on `cond_new` for each. Set a seed first. Store the result as `boot_slopes` and print it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-5-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(47)
boot_slopes <- mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

boot_slopes
```

###

A bootstrap sample draws 141 auctions with replacement from the 141 we have, so there is no null hypothesis to impose. Although we know there is a relationship between the condition of the game and its price, we might be more interested in the difference in price, here given by the slope of the linear regression line.

### Exercise 6

Replace the print with a summary of `boot_slopes`: the mean, the smallest and largest slopes, and the standard deviation of the slopes. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-6
```

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-6-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(47)
boot_slopes <- mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

boot_slopes |>
  summarize(mean = mean(stat),
            min = min(stat),
            max = max(stat),
            se = sd(stat))
```

###

The standard deviation of the bootstrap slopes, 1.22 for us, estimates the standard error of the slope. Reading its histogram by eye, the chapter takes 1.5 as a rough approximation of the standard error, while the regression table's formula gives 1.26.

### Exercise 7

Replace the summary so that it uses **infer** to calculate a 90% standard error confidence interval for the slope from `boot_slopes`, centered on the observed slope of 10.9. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-7-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(47)
boot_slopes <- mario |>
  specify(price ~ cond_new) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "slope")

boot_slopes |>
  get_confidence_interval(level = 0.90, type = "se", point_estimate = 10.9)
```

###

Ours runs from \$8.89 to \$12.90: 10.9 plus or minus 1.645 bootstrap standard errors. With its rough standard error of 1.5, the chapter concludes that for games that are new, the average price is higher by between \$8.43 and \$13.37 than games that are used, with 90% confidence.

### Exercise 8

Replace the interval with a 90% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the slope from `boot_slopes`. Render.


Because there were 1,000 bootstrap resamples, we look for the cutoffs which provide 50 bootstrap slopes on the left, 900 in the middle, and 50 on the right. Our cutoffs are \$8.94 and \$13.00, close to the chapter's \$9 to \$13.10, read from its histogram.

### Exercise 9

Replace the interval with a histogram of `boot_slopes`, with dashed vertical lines at the ends of the 90% percentile interval. Render.


The bootstrap slopes are bell-shaped and centered on 10.9, while the permuted slopes in Exercise 4 were centered on 0. Both intervals, \$8.89 to \$12.90 and \$8.94 to \$13.00, sit far above zero, which agrees with the permutation test.

Each fold holds 47 of the 141 auctions. We applied 3-fold cross-validation, so 1/3 of the data was removed while 2/3 of the observations were used to build each model.

### Exercise 11

Add code so that, for each fold, it fits the regression of `price` on `cond_new` to the other two folds, then predicts the price of each auction in the held-out fold and calculates its residual. Show the cross-validation sum of squared errors (CV SSE): the sum of all 141 squared residuals. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-11-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(4)
mario_folds <- mario |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n())))

map(1:3, \(k) lm(price ~ cond_new, data = filter(mario_folds, fold != k)) |>
      augment(newdata = filter(mario_folds, fold == k))) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  summarize(cv_sse = sum(.resid^2))
```

###

Our CV SSE for the one-predictor model is 7,923, and a different seed would put different auctions in each fold. Each prediction comes from a model built (using the other 2/3) without the observation (which is in the 1/3) being used.

### Exercise 12

Change the code so that it does the same for the four-predictor model too, storing every held-out prediction and residual from both models, labeled by model, as `mario_cv`. Show the CV SSE of each model. Render.

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: computational-approach-and-cross-validation-12-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(4)
mario_folds <- mario |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n())))

mario_cv <- bind_rows(
  "One predictor" = map(1:3, \(k) lm(price ~ cond_new,
                                     data = filter(mario_folds, fold != k)) |>
                          augment(newdata = filter(mario_folds, fold == k))) |>
    list_rbind(),
  "Four predictors" = map(1:3, \(k) lm(price ~ cond_new + stock_photo + duration + wheels,
                                       data = filter(mario_folds, fold != k)) |>
                            augment(newdata = filter(mario_folds, fold == k))) |>
    list_rbind(),
  .id = "model"
)

mario_cv |>
  summarize(cv_sse = sum(.resid^2), .by = model)
```

###

With four predictors, our CV SSE falls from 7,923 to 3,482. The CV SSE is smaller, by a factor of almost two, for the model with four predictors.

```{r}

set.seed(4)
mario_folds <- mario |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n())))

mario_cv <- bind_rows(
  "One predictor" = map(1:3, \(k) lm(price ~ cond_new,
                                     data = filter(mario_folds, fold != k)) |>

)

mario_cv |>

```

###

With one predictor, every prediction is one of just a few values, one for used games and one for new games in each fold, so the points form vertical stripes. The residuals give us a sense for how well the model will do at predicting observations which were not a part of the original dataset, e.g., future studies.

```{r}
set.seed(4)
mario_folds <- mario |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n())))

mario_cv <- bind_rows(

    list_rbind(),
  "Four predictors" = map(1:3, \(k) lm(price ~ cond_new + stock_photo + duration + wheels,

  labs(title = "Cross-Validated Errors for Two Models of Mario Kart Prices",

       color = "Fold",
       caption = "141 eBay auctions under $100, October 2009; 3-fold cross-validation")
```

###

The four-predictor errors stay within about \$14 of zero, while the one-predictor errors reach \$22. Using a single valued criterion (CV SSE) allows us to make a decision to choose the model with four predictors.

```{.output}
b71f3d2 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Simulate and cross-validate Mario Kart models
4e8a1c7 Model Mario Kart prices
9be04d2 Initial commit
```

Each time 1/3 of the data is removed, the resulting model will produce slightly different model coefficients. Cross-validation judges a model by the auctions it never saw, not by how well it fits the ones it did.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 27: Applications: Model and infer](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to fit and read one-predictor and multiple regression models of eBay auction prices for *Mario Kart*, to test and estimate a slope by permutation and by the bootstrap, and to compare two models with cross-validation.

This was the book's last chapter. To keep going, reread any part of [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) whose ideas you used here, from [Chapter 8: Linear regression with multiple predictors](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-mlr.html) to [Chapter 25: Inference for regression with multiple predictors](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-mlr.html), where cross-validation first appears. For one more case study, try the chapter's own R lab, [Multiple linear regression: Grading the professor](https://www.openintro.org/go?id=ims-r-lab-model-infer).

Many sentences in this tutorial come from the chapter, used under the book's [CC BY-SA 3.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).

````{verbatim}
```{r}
mario <- mariokart |>
  filter(total_pr < 100) |>
  mutate(price = total_pr,
         cond_new = if_else(cond == "new", 1, 0),

  select(price, cond_new, stock_photo, duration, wheels)

mario
```

```{r}
bind_rows(
  "One predictor" = lm(price ~ cond_new, data = mario) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE),
  "Four predictors" = lm(price ~ cond_new + stock_photo + duration + wheels,
                         data = mario) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model),
         term = fct_recode(term,
                           "New condition" = "cond_new",
                           "Stock photo" = "stock_photo",
                           "Each day of auction" = "duration",
                           "Each Wii wheel" = "wheels")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = term, y = estimate, color = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "What Adds to the Price of Mario Kart on eBay",
       subtitle = "Holding wheels and the rest constant cuts the premium for a new game from $10.90 to $5.13",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Change in Total Price, with 95% Confidence Interval",
       color = "Model",
       caption = "141 eBay auctions under $100, October 2009; two bundles removed") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
````
